text.p: These are the leading stories in the Turkish press on Friday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
SABAH
- Former prime minister Tansu Ciller denies working for the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency after a military court is authorised to investigate the allegation.
- Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz says at a meeting with trade union and business groups his government will not index salaries to inflation as proposed by the previous government.
MILLIYET
- The constitutional court turns down an Islamist Welfare Party request for an extra three months to prepare its written defence against charges which threaten it with closure.
- A report reveals that Turkish companies built up by women make less money but last longer.
HURRIYET
- A leading Turkish intelligence official is to be posted abroad after his name was linked to a security scandal which brought ties between the state and underworld gangs to light.
- The transport minister will brief the cabinet, opposition and media on the benefits of privatising Turk Telecom.
YENI YUZYIL
- The state searches for cars, mobile phones, videos and televison sets that were bought under the former Islamist-led government but have gone missing.
- The state will pay seven billion Turkish Lira ($45,000) to a patient who lost his arm because of a hospital's mistake.
RADIKAL
- The government will cut value-added-tax on everyday products and increase tax on luxury goods.
CUMHURIYET
- The finance minister and state minister responsible for the economy disagree over tax policies.
- An official report reveals that the number of unionised workers has dropped 1.04 percent from a year earlier.
DUNYA
- Representatives of leading sectors -- tourism, textile and readywear -- express their worries for the future and list their demands to the new government.
ZAMAN
- A draft law to increase secularist compulsory education to eight years from five is presented to Yilmaz.
($1 = 154,350 Turkish lira)
